context: Current closing price of Electronic Arts (EA): $200.97 USD as of 2026-05-22.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd infer was a current price around $201–202, with very little directional conviction at any horizon. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price, assuming mean-reverting intraday dynamics and no major scheduled catalysts. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to $202, reflecting a mild assumption of positive drift consistent with long-run equity risk premium, while acknowledging that a week is long enough for meaningful price discovery. At the one-month horizon, the $203 estimate again reflects little more than a slight upward drift assumption — essentially saying I have no strong view on direction and am leaning on the historical tendency of equities to drift modestly higher over time.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to typical realized volatility scaling. For a one-day window, a roughly ±2.5–3% band captures most normal trading-day outcomes. For one week, I widened to roughly ±5–6%, consistent with daily volatility compounding over five sessions. At one month, the ±10–11% band reflects approximately four weeks of volatility accumulation. These widths are grounded in historical equity volatility norms — not any specific instrument — and assume no structural breaks or regime changes during the forecast window.

Several sources of uncertainty influenced my interval widths beyond simple volatility scaling. Macro data releases, central bank communications, and earnings announcements (depending on the specific asset) can all cause sharp discontinuous moves. Liquidity conditions and broader risk-off episodes can amplify volatility well beyond baseline assumptions, particularly at the weekly and monthly horizons. I also incorporated some uncertainty about whether the prevailing volatility regime would persist or shift.

Tail risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a sudden geopolitical shock, an unexpected central bank policy pivot, or a systemic financial event that triggers broad de-risking. On the upside, a surprise earnings beat, strong macro data, or a major policy stimulus announcement could drive prices above my upper bounds. At the one-month horizon especially, the world can change substantially, and my intervals — while reasonably wide — remain conditioned on a roughly stable macro and market environment that could easily fail to materialize.
